l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Siguna is wife of Loki (she catches the serpent's venom in a cup)
q: His wife Siguna sits by his side and catches the drops as they fall, in a cup; but when she carries it away to empty it, the venom falls upon Loki, which makes him howl with horror, and twist his body about so violently that the whole earth shakes, and this produces what men call earthquakes.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Vidar is son of Odin
q: Odin, who engages the wolf Fenris, but falls a victim to the monster, who is, however, slain by Vidar, Odin's son.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: the gods are destroyed in Ragnarok (together with the visible creation)
q: It was a firm belief of the northern nations that a time would come when all the visible creation, the gods of Valhalla and Niffleheim, the inhabitants of Jotunheim, Alfheim, and Midgard, together with their habitations, would be destroyed.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: the gods fight at the battle of Vigrid (against the enemies of the gods)
q: But they, disregarding its fall, direct their course to the battle-field called Vigrid. Thither also repair the wolf Fenris, the Midgard serpent, Loki with all the followers of Hela, and the Frost giants.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Asgard is home of the gods
q: Hermod then rode back to Asgard and gave an account of all he had heard and witnessed.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Valhalla contains mistletoe (on its eastern side)
q: All things," replied Frigga, "except one little shrub that grows on the eastern side of Valhalla, and is called Mistletoe, and which I thought too young and feeble to crave an oath from."

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Balder is invulnerable to all things except mistletoe (after Frigga's oaths)
q: Ay," said Frigga, "neither stones, nor sticks, nor anything else can hurt Baldur, for I have exacted an oath from all of them. " "What," exclaimed the woman, "have all things sworn to spare Baldur?" "All things," replied Frigga, "except one little shrub that grows on the eastern side of Valhalla, and is called Mistletoe, and which I thought too young and feeble to crave an oath from."

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Hel is besought to let Balder
q: The next morning he besought Hela to let Baldur ride home with him, assuring her that nothing but lamentations were to be heard among the gods.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Alfheim is country of the Elves (the domain of Freyr)
q: Their country was called Alfheim, and was the domain of Freyr, the god of the sun, in whose light they were always sporting.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: mistletoe is a shrub (young and feeble; growing east of Valhalla)
q: All things," replied Frigga, "except one little shrub that grows on the eastern side of Valhalla, and is called Mistletoe, and which I thought too young and feeble to crave an oath from."

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: the Elves are a beings inferior to the gods (possessing great power)
q: The Edda mentions another class of beings, inferior to the gods, but still possessed of great power; these were called Elves.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: the Elves include the dwarfs (the black or Night Elves)
q: The black of Night Elves were a different kind of creatures. Ugly, long-nosed dwarfs, of a dirty brown color, they appeared only at night, for they avoided the sun as their most deadly enemy, because whenever his beams fell upon any of them they changed them immediately into stones.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: the Elves are exceedingly fair the white spirits (Elves of Light)
q: The white spirits, or Elves of Light, were exceedingly fair, more brilliant than the sun, and clad in garments of delicate and transparent texture.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Ragnarok is a destruction of the visible creation (the Twilight of the Gods)
q: It was a firm belief of the northern nations that a time would come when all the visible creation, the gods of Valhalla and Niffleheim, the inhabitants of Jotunheim, Alfheim, and Midgard, together with their habitations, would be destroyed.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Ragnarok is preceded by the triple winter (three winters without summer, followed by war and discord)
q: First will come a triple winter, during which snow will fall from the four corners of the heavens, the frost be very severe, the wind piercing, the weather tempestuous, and the sun impart no gladness.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Ragnarok ends with a new heaven and a new earth (created by Alfadur)
q: After this Alfadur (the almighty) will cause a new heaven and a new earth to arise out of the sea.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: the death of Baldur is caused by mistletoe (thrown by Hodur under Loki's guidance)
q: Hodur then took the mistletoe, and under the guidance of Loki, darted it at Baldur, who, pierced through and through, fell down lifeless.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Balder dies from mistletoe (pierced by it when thrown by Hodur)
q: Hodur then took the mistletoe, and under the guidance of Loki, darted it at Baldur, who, pierced through and through, fell down lifeless.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: the funeral of Baldur is borne to the sea-shore (the dead body)
q: The gods took up the dead body and bore it to the sea-shore where stood Baldur's ship Hringham, which passed for the largest in the world.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Runic characters consist of straight lines (almost invariably)
q: The letters consist almost invariably of straight lines, in the shape of little sticks either singly or put together.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Runic characters are used for magical purposes (especially in earlier times)
q: The Runic characters were of various kinds. They were chiefly used for magical purposes.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: the runes include bitter runes (used to bring evils on enemies)
q: The noxious, or, as they called them, the BITTER runes, were employed to bring various evils on their enemies; the favorable averted misfortune.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: the Skalds are a bards and poets (of the nation)
q: The Skalds were the bards and poets of the nation, a very important class of men in all communities in an early stage of civilization.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: the Skalds preserve historic lore (as depositaries of what history exists)
q: They are the depositaries of whatever historic lore there is, and it is their office to mingle something of intellectual gratification with the rude feasts of the warriors, by rehearsing, with such accompaniments of poetry and music as their skill can afford, the exploits of their heroes living or dead.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Sagas are composed by the Skalds
q: The compositions of the Skalds were called Sagas, many of which have come down to us, and contain valuable materials of history, and a faithful picture of the state of society at the time to which they relate.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: the Eddas come from Iceland (along with the Sagas)
q: The Eddas and Sagas have come to us from Iceland.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Iceland is a wild land of barrenness and lava (an island in the North Ocean)
q: In that strange island, Iceland, burst up, the geologists say, by fire from the bottom of the sea, a wild land of barrenness and lava, swallowed many months of every year in black tempests, yet with a wild, gleaming beauty in summer time, towering up there stern and grim in the North Ocean

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Balder is denied return from Hel (because Thaukt refuses to weep)
q: But she answered, "Thaukt will wail With dry tears Baldur's bale-fire. Let Hela keep her own."

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Balder is burned on the funeral pile (with Nanna)
q: Baldur's dead body was put on the funeral pile, on board the ship, and his wife Nanna was so struck with grief at the sight that she broke her heart, and her body was burned on the same pile with her husband's.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Odin consults Angerbode (the prophetess)
q: Odin, not satisfied with all this, and feeling alarmed for the fate of his son, determined to consult the prophetess Angerbode, a giantess, mother of Fenris, Hela, and the Midgard serpent.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Odin is father of Balder
q: Odin, not satisfied with all this, and feeling alarmed for the fate of his son, determined to consult the prophetess Angerbode, a giantess, mother of Fenris, Hela, and the Midgard serpent.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids is a priests or ministers of religion (among the ancient Celtic nations)
q: The Druids were the priests or ministers of religion among the ancient Celtic nations in Gaul, Britain, and Germany.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids worshipped inferior Gods (according to Latin writers)
q: The Latin writers assert that the Druids also worshipped numerous inferior Gods.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids used images no images (to represent the object of worship)
q: They used no images to represent the object of their worship, nor did they meet in temples or buildings of any kind for the performance of their sacred rites.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids has sacred place a circle of stones
q: A circle of stones (each stone generally of vast size) enclosing an area of from twenty feet to thirty yards in diameter, constituted their sacred place.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids used Cromlech (as a central altar in sacred circles)
q: In the centre of the circle stood the Cromlech or altar, which was a large stone, placed in the manner of a table upon other stones set up on end.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids used Cairns (as high places in sun worship)
q: The Druids had also their high places, which were large stones or piles of stones on the summits of hills. These were called Cairns, and were used in the worship of the deity under the symbol of the sun.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids offered sacrifices (to their deity)
q: That the Druids offered sacrifices to their deity there can be no doubt.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids practiced human sacrifice (according to classical Roman writers on great occasions)
q: The classical (Roman) writers affirm that they offered on great occasions human sacrifices; as for success in war or for relief from dangerous diseases.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids observed Beltane (as an annual festival in the beginning of May)
q: The Druids observed two festivals in each year. The former took place in the beginning of May, and was called Beltane or "fire of God."

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids observed Samh'in (as an annual festival on Hallow-eve)
q: The other great festival of the Druids was called "Samh'in," or "fire of peace," and was held on Hallow-eve (first of November)

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids held judicial conclaves Samh'in (during the festival)
q: On this occasion the Druids assembled in solemn conclave, in the most central part of the district, to discharge the judicial functions of their order.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids served ancient Celtic nations (as religious ministers)
q: The Druids were the priests or ministers of religion among the ancient Celtic nations in Gaul, Britain, and Germany.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids observed full moon (especially the sixth day of the moon)
q: Besides these two great annual festivals, the Druids were in the habit of observing the full moon, and especially the sixth day of the moon.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids sought mistletoe (on the sixth day of the moon)
q: On the latter they sought the mistletoe, which grew on their favorite oaks, and to which, as well as to the oak itself, they ascribed a peculiar virtue and sacredness.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids taught morality (as well as religion)
q: The Druids were the teachers of morality as well as of religion.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids were men of science and learning (of their age and people)
q: They were also the men of science and learning of their age and people.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids preserved teaching orally oral tradition (without committing doctrine, history, or poetry to writing)
q: But it is certain that they committed nothing of their doctrine, their history, or their poetry to writing. Their teaching was oral, and their literature (if such a word may be used in such a case) was preserved solely by tradition.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids taught stars, world, lands, and gods (according to Roman writers)
q: But the Roman writers admit that "they paid much attention to the order and laws of nature, and investigated and taught to the youth under their charge many things concerning the stars and their motions, the size of the world and the lands , and concerning the might and power of the immortal gods."

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids preserved history as traditional tales (celebrating the heroic deeds of forefathers)
q: Their history consisted in traditional tales, in which the heroic deeds of their forefathers were celebrated.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids included Bards (as an essential part of their hierarchy)
q: The Bards were an essential part of the Druidical hierarchy.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids reached height Roman invasion (under Julius Caesar)
q: The Druidical system was at its height at the time of the Roman invasion under Julius Caesar.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids retreated to Iona (after Roman persecution on the mainland)
q: The Druids, harassed at all points on the main-land, retreated to Anglesey and Iona, where for a season they found shelter, and continued their now-dishonored rites.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids combined functions priest, magistrate, scholar, and physician
q: The Druids combined the functions of the priest, the magistrate, the scholar, and the physician.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids retained predominance in Iona (until supplanted by St. Columba)
q: The Druids retained their predominance in Iona and over the adjacent islands and main-land until they were supplanted and their superstitions overturned by the arrival of St. Columba

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Iona provided shelter to The Druids (for a season after their retreat)
q: The Druids, harassed at all points on the main-land, retreated to Anglesey and Iona, where for a season they found shelter, and continued their now-dishonored rites.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Bards is a essential part of the Druidical hierarchy
q: The Bards were an essential part of the Druidical hierarchy.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Bards served as oral historians (of public and private transactions)
q: The bards were supposed to be endowed with powers equal to inspiration. They were the oral historians of all past transactions, public and private.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Bards served as genealogists (accomplished)
q: They were also accomplished genealogists.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Bards held Eisteddfods (in Wales for many centuries)
q: Pennant gives a minute account of the Eisteddfods or sessions of the bards and minstrels, which were held in Wales for many centuries, long after the Druidical priesthood in its other departments became extinct.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: St. Columba is a apostle of the Highlands
q: The Druids retained their predominance in Iona and over the adjacent islands and main-land until they were supplanted and their superstitions overturned by the arrival of St. Columba, the apostle of the Highlands

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: St. Columba led inhabitants to profess Christianity (in the Highlands and adjacent district)
q: by whom the inhabitants of that district were first led to profess Christianity.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Highlands was evangelized by St. Columba (as apostle)
q: The Druids retained their predominance in Iona and over the adjacent islands and main-land until they were supplanted and their superstitions overturned by the arrival of St. Columba, the apostle of the Highlands

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Christianity was professed by inhabitants of the Highlands (first led by St. Columba)
q: by whom the inhabitants of that district were first led to profess Christianity.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids held relation analogous to Brahmans (in relation to the Celtic peoples)
q: They stood to the people of the Celtic tribes in a relation closely analogous to that in which the Brahmans of India, the Magi of Persia, and the priests of the Egyptians stood to the people respectively by whom they were revered.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids held relation analogous to Magi of Persia (in relation to the Celtic peoples)
q: They stood to the people of the Celtic tribes in a relation closely analogous to that in which the Brahmans of India, the Magi of Persia, and the priests of the Egyptians stood to the people respectively by whom they were revered.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids held relation analogous to priests of the Egyptians (in relation to the Celtic peoples)
q: They stood to the people of the Celtic tribes in a relation closely analogous to that in which the Brahmans of India, the Magi of Persia, and the priests of the Egyptians stood to the people respectively by whom they were revered.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids taught existence of one God
q: The Druids taught the existence of one God, to whom they gave a name "Be'al," which Celtic antiquaries tell us means "the life of everything," or "the source of all beings,:"

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids called supreme deity Be'al
q: The Druids taught the existence of one God, to whom they gave a name "Be'al," which Celtic antiquaries tell us means "the life of everything," or "the source of all beings,:"

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids identified supreme deity with the Sun (as did the Phoenicians)
q: What renders this affinity more striking is that the Druids as well as the Phoenicians identified this, their supreme deity, with the Sun.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Iona is one of the British Isles (one of the smallest)
q: One of the smallest of the British Isles, situated near a ragged and barren coast, surrounded by dangerous seas, and possessing no sources of internal wealth, Iona has obtained an imperishable place in history as the seat of civilization and religion at a time when the darkness of heathenism hung over almost the whole of Northern Europe.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: western and northern parts of Scotland has state heathenism (at the time of Columba)
q: while the western and northern parts of Scotland were still immersed in the darkness of heathenism.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Columba's landing on Iona occurs in 563 (in the year of our Lord)
q: Columba, with twelve friends landed on the island of Iona in the year of our Lord 563

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: St. Columba lands on Iona (with twelve friends)
q: Columba, with twelve friends landed on the island of Iona in the year of our Lord 563

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: St. Columba travels in wicker boat (covered with hides)
q: having made the passage in a wicker boat covered with hides.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: The Druids oppose settlement of St. Columba (on Iona)
q: The Druids who occupied the island endeavored to prevent his settling there

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: St. Columba receives Iona (as a gift from the king)
q: procured from the king a gift of the island

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: St. Columba establishes monastery of Iona (on Iona)
q: and established there a monastery of which he was the abbot.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: St. Columba is a presbyter (not a bishop)
q: though not a bishop, but merely a presbyter and monk

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: St. Columba is a monk (not a bishop)
q: though not a bishop, but merely a presbyter and monk

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: St. Columba disseminates Scriptures (throughout the Highlands and Islands of Scotland)
q: He was unwearied in his labors to disseminate a knowledge of the Scriptures throughout the Highlands and Islands of Scotland

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Iona is also called Icolmkill
q: Iona or Icolmkill is situated at the extremity of the island of Mull

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: St. Columba has authority over bishops (throughout the entire province)
q: the entire province with its bishops was subject to him and his successors.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pictish monarch honors St. Columba (in the highest honor)
q: The Pictish monarch was so impressed with a sense of his wisdom and worth that he held him in the highest honor

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: neighboring chiefs and princes seek counsel from St. Columba (for settling disputes)
q: the neighboring chiefs and princes sought his counsel and availed themselves of his judgment in settling their disputes.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: twelve followers of Columba forms Culdees (Columba was the head)
q: When Columba landed on Iona he was attended by twelve followers whom he had formed into a religious body, of which he was the head.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Culdees is a religious persons (associated for common religious work)
q: They were a body of religious persons associated together for the purpose of aiding each other in the common work of preaching the gospel and teaching youth

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Culdee system is called monastery (with its superior called an abbot)
q: Their institution was called a monastery, and the superior an abbot

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Culdee system requires obedience (among the three traditional monastic vows)
q: of these, which are three, celibacy, poverty, and obedience, the Culdees were bound to none except the third.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Culdees are not bound to poverty (they labored to procure comforts of life)
q: To poverty they did not bind themselves; on the contrary, they seem to have labored diligently to procure for themselves and those dependent on them the comforts of life.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Culdees permit marriage (for members of the order)
q: Marriage also was allowed them, and most of them seem to have entered into that state.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Culdee system has wives residing at Eilen nam ban (when husbands served at the school or sanctuary)
q: Near Iona there is an island which still bears the name of "Eilen nam ban," women's island, where their husbands seem to have resided with them, except when duty required their presence in the school or the sanctuary.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Iona is situated at Mull (at the island's extremity)
q: Iona or Icolmkill is situated at the extremity of the island of Mull

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Culdees are deemed heretical (because they departed from Romish Church rules)
q: In these respects and in others the Culdees departed from the established rules of the Romish Church, and consequently were deemed heretical.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Roman Catholic Church enfeebles Culdees (as its power advances)
q: as the power of the latter advanced, that of the Culdees was enfeebled.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Culdees resist papal usurpation (as individuals after suppression)
q: They still continued to labor as individuals, and resisted the inroads of Papa usurpation as they best might till the light of the Reformation dawned on the world.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Iona contains nunnery on Iona (under the reign of Popery)
q: Under the reign of Popery the island became the seat of a nunnery, the ruins of which are still seen.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: nunnery on Iona is dismantled at Reformation (the nuns were allowed to remain in community)
q: At the Reformation, the nuns were allowed to remain, living in community, when the abbey was dismantled.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Iona is resorted to by travellers (for ecclesiastical and sepulchral remains)
q: Ionia is now chiefly resorted to by travellers on account of the numerous ecclesiastical and sepulchral remains which are found upon it.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Iona contains Cathedral or Abbey Church (principal ecclesiastical remain)
q: The principal of these are the Cathedral or Abbey Church, and the Chapel of the Nunnery.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Iona is separated from Mull (by a strait half a mile wide)
q: from which it is separated by a strait of half a mile in breadth

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Iona contains Chapel of the Nunnery (principal ecclesiastical remain)
q: The principal of these are the Cathedral or Abbey Church, and the Chapel of the Nunnery.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Staffa is opposite Iona (across the sea)
q: In the Lord of the Isles, Scott beautifully contrasts the church on Iona with the Cave of Staffa, opposite:

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Iona is distant from mainland of Scotland (thirty-six miles)
q: its distance from the main-land of Scotland being thirty-six miles.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Iona is a seat of civilization (during the spread of heathenism in Northern Europe)
q: Iona has obtained an imperishable place in history as the seat of civilization and religion at a time when the darkness of heathenism hung over almost the whole of Northern Europe.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Iona is a seat of religion (during the spread of heathenism in Northern Europe)
q: Iona has obtained an imperishable place in history as the seat of civilization and religion at a time when the darkness of heathenism hung over almost the whole of Northern Europe.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: St. Columba is a native of Ireland
q: Columba was a native of Ireland, and connected by birth with the princes of the land.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Python is a enormous serpent
q: Among the rest, Python, an enormous serpent, crept forth, the terror of the people, and lurked in the caves of Mount Parnassus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Apollo is a god of music, poetry, and medicine
q: Apollo was god of music and of poetry and also of medicine.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Apollo is son of Jupiter
q: Jupiter is my father, and I am lord of Delphos and Tenedos, and know all things, present and future.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Apollo loves Daphne (after Cupid strikes him with the golden arrow)
q: Forthwith the god was seized with love for the maiden, and she abhorred the thought of loving.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Apollo adopts as tree laurel tree (after Daphne is transformed)
q: Since you cannot be my wife," said he, "you shall assuredly be my tree. I will wear you for my crown.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Cupid is a Venus's boy
q: Venus's boy heard these words, and rejoined, ":Your arrows may strike all things else, Apollo, but mine shall strike you.:"

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Cupid causes Apollo and Daphne (by striking Daphne with a leaden arrow and Apollo with a golden arrow)
q: With the leaden shaft he struck the nymph Daphne, the daughter of the river god Peneus, and with the golden one Apollo, through the heart.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Daphne is a nymph
q: With the leaden shaft he struck the nymph Daphne, the daughter of the river god Peneus, and with the golden one Apollo, through the heart.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Daphne is daughter of Peneus
q: With the leaden shaft he struck the nymph Daphne, the daughter of the river god Peneus, and with the golden one Apollo, through the heart.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Python lurks in Parnassus (in caves)
q: Among the rest, Python, an enormous serpent, crept forth, the terror of the people, and lurked in the caves of Mount Parnassus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Daphne rejects marriage (she wishes to remain unmarried like Diana)
q: She, hating the thought of marriage as a crime, with her beautiful face tinged all over with blushes, threw her arms around her father's neck, and said, "Dearest father, grant me this favor, that I may always remain unmarried, like Diana."

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Daphne becomes laurel tree (after praying to Peneus for transformation)
q: The nymph, now changed into a laurel tree, bowed its head in grateful acknowledgment.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: laurel tree remains green eternal youth (by Apollo's promise)
q: And, as eternal youth is mine, you also shall be always green, and your leaf know no decay."

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pyramus is a handsome youth (the handsomest youth in Babylonia)
q: Pyramus was the handsomest youth, and Thisbe the fairest maiden, in all Babylonia, where Semiramis reigned.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Thisbe is a fair maiden (the fairest maiden in Babylonia)
q: Pyramus was the handsomest youth, and Thisbe the fairest maiden, in all Babylonia, where Semiramis reigned.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pyramus loves Thisbe (their parents forbid their marriage)
q: One thing, however, they could not forbid that love should glow with equal ardor in the bosoms of both.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pyramus and Thisbe are separated by a crack (between the adjoining houses)
q: In the wall that parted the two houses there was a crack, caused by some fault in the structure.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Thisbe possesses Thisbe's veil (she drops it while fleeing the lioness)
q: As she fled she dropped her veil.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Thisbe flees lioness (after seeing it at the fountain)
q: As she sat alone in the dim light of the evening she descried a lioness, her jaws reeking with recent slaughter, approaching the fountain to slake her thirst. Thisbe fled at the sight, and sought refuge in the hollow of a rock.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: lioness tears Thisbe's veil (with her bloody mouth)
q: The lioness, after drinking at the spring, turned to retreat to the woods, and seeing the veil on the ground, tossed and rent it with her bloody mouth.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Apollo slays Python (with his arrows)
q: Apollo slew him with his arrows weapons which he had not before used against any but feeble animals, hares, wild goats, and such game.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pyramus possesses Pyramus's sword
q: He took up the veil, carried it with him to the appointed tree, and covered it with kisses and with tears. "My blood also shall stain your texture," said he, and drawing his sword plunged it into his heart.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: the tomb of Ninus is located outside Babylonia (outside the city’s bounds)
q: Then, after lamenting their hard fate, they agreed that next night, when all was still, they would slip away from watchful eyes, leave their dwellings and walk out into the fields; and to insure a meeting, repair to a well-known edifice, standing without the city's bounds, called the tomb of Ninus

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Cephalus is a beautiful youth (fond of manly sports)
q: Cephalus was a beautiful youth and fond of manly sports.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Cephalus is married to Procris (he loves her devotedly)
q: But Cephalus was just married to a charming wife whom he loved devotedly. Her name was Procris.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Aurora loves Cephalus (she steals him away but he resists her)
q: Aurora saw him when she first looked forth, fell in love with him, and stole him away.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Procris is favorite of Diana
q: She was a favorite of Diana, the goddess of hunting, who had given her a dog which could outrun every rival, and a javelin which would never fail of its mark; and Procris gave these presents to her husband.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Procris possesses Procris's javelin (the javelin never fails to hit its mark)
q: She was a favorite of Diana, the goddess of hunting, who had given her a dog which could outrun every rival, and a javelin which would never fail of its mark; and Procris gave these presents to her husband.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Lelaps is owned by Cephalus (the dog is given to Procris by Diana and then given to her husband)
q: She was a favorite of Diana, the goddess of hunting, who had given her a dog which could outrun every rival, and a javelin which would never fail of its mark; and Procris gave these presents to her husband.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Apollo institutes Pythian games (to commemorate his conquest of Python)
q: In commemoration of this illustrious conquest he instituted the Pythian games, in which the victor in feats of strength, swiftness of foot, or in the chariot race, was crowned with a wreath of beech leaves; for the laurel was not yet adopted by Apollo as his own tree.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: the fox is a ravenous fox (sent to annoy the country)
q: Now it happened some angry deity had sent a ravenous fox to annoy the country; and the hunters turned out in great strength to capture it.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Cephalus and Procris wounds Procris (with the weapon)
q: A cry from his beloved Procris told him that the weapon had too surely met its mark.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Procris is wounded by the javelin (her own gift)
q: He rushed to the place, and found her bleeding and with sinking strength endeavoring to draw forth from the wound the javelin, her own gift.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: the breeze is mistaken for a lover (by an informer who deceives Procris)
q: Some one passing by one day heard him talking in this way to the air, and, foolishly believing that he was talking to some maiden, went and told the secret to Procris, Cephalus's wife.
